passage: Everyone in Class 9 knew me: I'm the boy who lends pens and carries the cricket kit. When the captain election was announced, I told myself the votes were already mine. I made no poster and wrote no speech, and on nomination day I skipped the class visits to play cricket. Gurleen, my rival, went from room to room with a two-line promise about a working water cooler and a library corner, and she even visited the Class 6 and 7 rows, which I had never thought of. On result day my friends were shocked. I lost by forty votes. I sat on the steps thinking: they liked me, but nobody knew what I would do. I'm Sandeep, and I have not forgotten that feeling.

qa.q: By how many votes did Sandeep lose?
qa.a: Sandeep lost by forty votes.

qa.q: What was Sandeep feeling on the steps, and what did the loss show?
qa.a: Sandeep felt shocked and let down, and saw that being liked was not enough because nobody knew what Sandeep would do.

qa.q: What could Sandeep have done differently, and why?
qa.a: Sandeep could have visited every class with one clear proposal and asked what students needed, because votes follow a plan people can picture.

qa.q: How might a Class 7 student have seen the two candidates?
qa.a: A Class 7 student would have seen Gurleen visit and speak clearly, while Sandeep never came, so Gurleen would seem the more serious choice.

grounding: A well-liked student assumes friends will vote for them and makes no plan, and rivals with clear proposals reach more classes, so the student loses despite a lot of goodwill.

subtype: Approach: writing and rehearsing the speech [Action]
passage: Hafsa, you're nervous about tomorrow's speech, so listen to your Baljeet Uncle. At sixteen I stood for house captain. I wrote my speech on the back of a calendar page. One promise: proper drainage so the ground would not flood during monsoon practice. One story: the day my shoes floated away in the middle of a football match. I read it to the mirror every night. Then I read it to my friend Gulshan, who timed me on his watch: three minutes ten. Too long. I cut every "as we all know" and "respected teachers and friends," and got it down to two minutes flat. On the day, the hall laughed at the shoes and remembered the drainage. I won by a small margin, and Gulshan claimed half the credit.

qa.q: What was the one promise in Baljeet's speech?
qa.a: The promise was proper drainage so the ground would not flood during monsoon practice.

qa.q: How might Baljeet have felt while reading to the mirror each night, and what does it show?
qa.a: Baljeet was probably nervous but determined, shown by the nightly practice and the willingness to be timed and corrected.

qa.q: What choice in the story shortened the speech, and why did it help?
qa.a: Cutting the filler phrases brought it to two minutes, because a shorter speech keeps the one promise and the story clear.

qa.q: How did Gulshan help in the story?
qa.a: Gulshan timed the speech on his watch and showed that it was too long at three minutes ten.

grounding: The candidate drafts a two-minute speech with one clear promise and one story, practises before a mirror and a friend, and trims filler after timing it.

subtype: Approach: promising things outside the role's power [Pitfall]
passage: The assembly hall was hot, the microphone squealed, and each candidate had ninety seconds. Mehak looked at the restless rows and decided ordinary promises would not be heard. "If I'm captain: no homework on Fridays! And free trips to the water park every term!" The hall roared. She grinned, dizzy with it. Behind the stage, Bhupen Sir, the civics teacher, frowned. "A captain can't cancel homework or approve trips, Mehak. Those aren't yours to promise." By the next day, students who had cheered were saying, "She can't do that." A Class 10 student told her, "I'd rather vote for someone who tells the truth." Mehak's stomach turned. She had won the applause and lost something she had not known she needed.

qa.q: How long did each candidate have to speak?
qa.a: Each candidate had ninety seconds.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel after the applause, and how did it change?
qa.a: Mehak felt dizzy and pleased at first, but her stomach turned once students began doubting her and a Class 10 student asked for honesty.

qa.q: What could Mehak have promised instead, and why?
qa.a: Mehak could have promised things a captain can do, such as asking staff about a sports-day slot and setting up a suggestion box, because those can be delivered and keep trust.

qa.q: How does Bhupen Sir see the promises?
qa.a: Bhupen Sir sees claims that cannot be delivered, which would harm Mehak's credibility with teachers and with students who value honesty.

grounding: The candidate promises no homework and free trips, and the claims win applause but cannot be delivered, harming credibility with teachers and with students who value honesty.

subtype: Approach: analogy with past successful candidates [Thinking]
passage: Manoj spread last year's election posters on the veranda of the kasba school and wrote one question: why did Sunaina Didi win? Not the speech, he decided. The water coolers. In her first month she had got the two broken coolers repaired and hung a small board reading "Fixed." Everyone saw it every day, and trust followed. Small, visible, quick. So, what is my cooler? Manoj walked the school with a notebook. The Class 8 fans were dead, the library door hung on one hinge, and the football goal had no net. He asked the peon what each repair would cost and how long it took, then picked the two he could honestly promise: the fans and the net. "A promise people can see by Friday," he wrote.

qa.q: What did Sunaina Didi have repaired in her first month?
qa.a: She had the two broken water coolers repaired.

qa.q: What is Manoj thinking about why Sunaina Didi won, and what does he want?
qa.a: Manoj thinks that visible small fixes earned trust, and he wants to find his own quick, honest promises.

qa.q: What else could Manoj do to test his two promises, and why?
qa.a: Manoj could ask the headmaster whether the fans and net can be fixed, because a promise only helps if the person in charge agrees it can be kept.

qa.q: How might a Class 8 student see the plan to fix the fans?
qa.a: A Class 8 student would likely feel noticed and hopeful, since the dead fans are something they sit under every day.

grounding: The student studies why a previous captain won, noting that visible small fixes such as repairing water coolers earned trust, and adapts that approach to current needs.

subtype: Approach: fair campaigning and respectful rivalry [Thinking]
passage: Nilesh's helpers had a plan on the canteen bench: someone would "accidentally" mention that the other candidate copied answers in the unit test. "It'll win us Class 9," one said. Nilesh put down his samosa. "No." The bench went quiet. "If I say that about someone, true or not, I'm asking for votes with a stone in my hand. I'd rather lose talking about library timings." One helper rolled his eyes and left. Later I saw Nilesh shake the other candidate's hand in the corridor and say good luck. I can't tell what he was thinking. He looked tired, not proud. - Ojas

qa.q: Where was the plan about the other candidate made?
qa.a: The plan was made on the canteen bench.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have felt when refusing the plan, and how sure can Ojas be?
qa.a: Nilesh probably felt firm but weary, since Nilesh looked tired and not proud, though Ojas cannot know what was thought.

qa.q: What could Nilesh's helpers do instead to win votes, and why?
qa.a: They could visit classes to talk about library timings, because a campaign built on ideas keeps friendships intact.

qa.q: How might the other candidate feel on getting the handshake?
qa.a: The other candidate probably feels surprised and respected, having no idea a rumour had been suggested.

grounding: The candidate decides not to mock opponents or spread rumours, reasoning that a campaign built on ideas keeps friendships intact and reflects the leadership being asked for.

subtype: Approach: handling nerves through practice and breathing [Action]
passage: Note, assembly, Class 10A. I stood by the stage steps for Parul's speech. Before her turn I saw her stop at the wing and breathe out slowly, counting four for each breath. She held a small card with three points in big letters. On stage her hands shook a little, but she found Amandeep in the third row, nodding, and spoke to that face. She lost her place once, glanced at the card and carried on. What I did: stayed until she finished, told her the pause was fine, and asked her to keep the card for the next event. I do not know how nervous she felt inside. I saw the breathing and the card.

qa.q: How many points were on Parul's card?
qa.a: The card had three points in big letters.

qa.q: What might Parul have felt before the speech, and how sure can the teacher be?
qa.a: Parul was probably nervous, since the hands shook and the breathing was slow and counted, though the teacher cannot know what was felt inside.

qa.q: What else could Parul do to prepare for next time, and why?
qa.a: Parul could practise aloud in the empty hall with a timer, because rehearsing in the real space makes the stage feel familiar.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt being the face Parul looked at?
qa.a: Amandeep may have felt proud to help and a little nervous, wanting to keep nodding steadily.

grounding: Before the assembly, the candidate slows breathing, holds a card with three key points and looks at a friendly face in the crowd, so anxiety does not wipe out the message.

subtype: Approach: learning from a loss and following through [Revision]
passage:
Sarita: Rajni, congratulations. Seriously.
Rajni: Thanks. You lost by seven votes, Sarita. I keep thinking about it.
Sarita: I did. And it stings, I won't pretend. Can I ask you something? What did you do that I didn't?
Rajni: Honestly? The Class 6 visits. You never came.
Sarita: Fair. Noted. And my canteen promise, I still want to do it.
Rajni: The queues?
Sarita: Yes. Can I lead a canteen committee under you? I'll do the work, you'll have the say.
Rajni: You'd do that?
Sarita: I said I'd fix the queues. Losing doesn't change that.
Rajni: Then yes. First meeting Monday at recess.

qa.q: By how many votes did Sarita lose?
qa.a: Sarita lost by seven votes.

qa.q: How does Sarita feel about the loss?
qa.a: Sarita feels stung but determined, admitting the loss hurts yet still wanting to keep the canteen promise.

qa.q: What could Sarita do if the committee moves slowly, and why?
qa.a: Sarita could ask for one small visible fix in the first month, because a quick result keeps helpers interested and shows the promise is real.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel about Sarita's offer?
qa.a: Rajni is probably surprised and respectful, since Sarita accepted the result and turned the loss into work.

grounding: After losing by a few votes, the student congratulates the winner, asks for feedback and offers to lead a canteen committee, turning the defeat into a way of doing the promised work anyway.

passage:
Hi Salma,

You were right to make me talk to the Class 7s. I have been telling everyone about library timings, but on Tuesday at the ground three Class 7 kids told me the sports period gets cancelled whenever it rains or there's a test, and it is never made up. I had never thought of it. So I have changed the speech. New line: "One sports period a week fixed on the timetable, and if it is cancelled, made up within the week." I'll ask the PT teacher whether that is possible before I promise anything. Could you listen to the new version at lunch and time it? It still has to fit in two minutes.

Hemant

qa.q: What did the three Class 7 kids say about sports periods?
qa.a: They said the sports period gets cancelled whenever it rains or there is a test, and it is never made up.

qa.q: What made Hemant change the speech, and how did Hemant feel about it?
qa.a: Hemant was surprised and interested, since Hemant had never thought of the sports periods until the Class 7 kids raised them.

qa.q: What else could Hemant do before promising the schedule, and why?
qa.a: Hemant could ask the PT teacher what is possible, because a promise is only worth making if the person in charge can agree to it.

qa.q: How might a Class 7 student see the new line in the speech?
qa.a: A Class 7 student would likely feel heard, since the complaint they raised on Tuesday became a promise. 🙂

grounding: Mid-campaign, the candidate notices younger students care most about sports periods and revises the speech to include a schedule proposal, showing that listening can reshape a plan in progress.

subtype: Approach: breaking the project into tasks and owners [Action]
passage: Their teacher in Rotterdam had given the class three weeks to build a working model of a wind turbine. Zeynep wrote four words on the whiteboard: Research, Materials, Construction, Presentation. Ingrid loved reading, so she took research. Jamal, who sawed straight and knew it, took construction. Pieter, the talkative one, took presentation. Zeynep kept materials and the calendar for herself. Next to each name went a date: summary by day five, materials by day eight, building from day nine to fifteen, rehearsal on day eighteen. "Everyone has one thing, and a date," she said. On day five Ingrid's summary was on the wall, and Jamal had already sanded his pieces of wood.

qa.q: What was the model the class had to build?
qa.a: The class had to build a working model of a wind turbine.

qa.q: What did Zeynep want from giving each person one task and one date?
qa.a: Zeynep wanted everyone to know what is expected of them, so that the work would not depend on others guessing.

qa.q: What could Zeynep do if someone falls behind on a date, and why?
qa.a: Zeynep could check in halfway to the date and offer to swap a small piece of work, because an early conversation is easier than a late rescue.

qa.q: How might Jamal see the task of construction?
qa.a: Jamal likely feels pleased and confident, since it matches what Jamal does best.

grounding: A team building a science model lists research, materials, construction and presentation, gives each member a task matching their strengths, and sets a date for each stage.

passage: In the school design lab, Lavanya looked at the tasks on the board for the model bridge: paint, wire the lights, test, build the frame. Vijay was ready to paint. "Not yet," said Lavanya. "Paint needs a dry frame, and the test can't happen until the wiring is done. Those two start the chain." She drew arrows: frame, then dry, then paint; circuit, then test. "Frame glue first, today, because it needs a whole day to dry. Circuit tomorrow. Meanwhile, Vijay, you can do the signboard and the poster. Nothing waits on those." Vijay shrugged, then began cutting card, his tongue between his teeth. By Friday the frame was dry and painted, and the little lights blinked on the first try.

qa.q: Why could Vijay not start painting at once?
qa.a: Painting needs a dry frame, and the frame glue needed a whole day to dry.

qa.q: How does Vijay feel when told not to paint yet?
qa.a: Vijay is a little reluctant and shrugs, but settles into the signboard work with concentration.

qa.q: What could Lavanya do if the glue takes longer than a day to dry, and why?
qa.a: Lavanya could move other tasks such as the poster and the wiring ahead while waiting, because independent jobs can run in parallel.

qa.q: How might Vijay see Lavanya's arrows?
qa.a: Vijay may see them as clear and fair once the reason is explained, since the arrows show why the painting comes later and what to do meanwhile.

grounding: The leader sees that painting cannot start until the frame dries and testing needs a working circuit, so she starts those tasks first and lets independent ones run in parallel.
